strategy_title: Add XBLOCK=64 num_warps=2 config to cut scheduler stalls further
strategy_description: When CPIStall 'not selected' stalls remain dominant after a prior round of num_warps reduction, adding an even smaller XBLOCK config (XBLOCK=64, num_warps=2) to the autotune search space can yield further improvement. In this case, the autotuner selected XBLOCK=64/num_warps=2 (32 threads/block), reducing active warps per scheduler from 8.73 to 6.88, Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction from 11.62 to 9.91, and executed instructions from 7.59M to 6.81M, producing a 1.77x speedup. Critically, the grid must be a lambda over meta['XBLOCK'] so the smaller block size actually reduces grid granularity; registers per thread also dropped from 32 to 30, slightly improving occupancy headroom.
fast_pseudocode:
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 64},  num_warps=2, num_stages=1),  # NEW: smallest block
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=2, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 256}, num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 512}, num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 512}, num_warps=8, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 1024}, num_warps=8, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 1024}, num_warps=16, num_stages=1),
    ],
    key=['xnumel'],
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    ...
grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)
kernel[grid](...)  # autotuner selects XBLOCK=64/num_warps=2 -> 6.88 active warps/scheduler
applicable_when: NCU CPIStall 'not selected' fraction remains >30% of stall cycles after prior num_warps reduction; active warps per scheduler still exceeds eligible warps per scheduler by >1.5x; waves_per_sm > 5 so smaller blocks won't starve SMs; kernel is pointwise/elementwise with no shared memory tiling; autotune config set does not yet include XBLOCK=64.
do_not_apply_when: waves_per_sm is low (<3) — reducing block size to 64 threads will leave SMs idle; kernel is memory-bound (Memory SOL > Compute SOL); kernel uses shared memory tiling where block size determines tile coverage; XBLOCK=64 configs are already present in the autotune search space.
framework_notes: In Triton, XBLOCK=64 with num_warps=2 yields 64 threads/block (2 warps). The grid lambda must use meta['XBLOCK'] to correctly shrink the grid. On Hopper (4 warp schedulers per SM), 2 warps/block means 0.5 warps/scheduler per block; with multiple co-resident blocks the effective active warps/scheduler settles around 6-7, which is closer to the eligible warp count and reduces 'not selected' stall fraction.

strategy_title: Add low-num_warps autotune configs to reduce scheduler contention
strategy_description: When the CPIStall 'not selected' stall type dominates (>30% of stall cycles) and active warps per scheduler significantly exceeds eligible warps per scheduler (ratio >1.5x), adding smaller num_warps configs (e.g., num_warps=2 alongside existing num_warps=4+) to the @triton.autotune search space allows the autotuner to select a configuration with fewer competing warps per scheduler. This reduces scheduler contention without starving the GPU, provided waves/SM remains above ~5. The profiling metrics here show only marginal improvement in the NCU metrics (Duration 16.26→16.16 us, Occupancy 54.7→58.4%), suggesting the autotuner may have selected a config that was already near-optimal for this kernel state, but the overall end-to-end speedup of 1.75x indicates the autotune search found a better configuration across the full workload.

applicable_when: CPIStall 'not selected' fraction >30% of total stall cycles; active warps per scheduler / eligible warps per scheduler ratio >1.5x; waves/SM >5 (GPU will not be starved by reducing block size); pointwise or elementwise kernel with no shared memory dependencies; existing autotune configs have minimum num_warps >= 4.
do_not_apply_when: Waves/SM < 3 (reducing block size may starve the GPU); kernel uses shared memory that requires a minimum number of warps for correctness or performance; the kernel is memory-bound rather than compute-bound (scheduler contention is not the bottleneck); the launch grid is not updated to a lambda over meta['XBLOCK'] (hardcoded grid causes redundant computation when XBLOCK changes).
framework_notes: In Triton, when adding or modifying @triton.autotune configs that vary XBLOCK, the launch grid MUST be a lambda: `grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)`. A static grid tuple will not adapt to the chosen XBLOCK and will cause each element to be processed multiple times. Do NOT pass XBLOCK as an explicit kwarg at the call site when @triton.autotune is active — autotune injects it automatically. The num_warps=2 configs correspond to 64 threads/block (2 warps × 32 threads).

strategy_title: PID swizzle halves branch instructions, reduces warp stall cycles
strategy_description: Applying a GROUP_SIZE=16 program-ID swizzle to a kernel with WorkloadImbalance (>5% max/avg active cycle ratio) and 5.1 waves/SM halved branch instructions (86K→43K) and reduced warp cycles per issued instruction from 9.91 to 9.35, yielding a 1.75x end-to-end speedup despite the per-kernel NCU duration being nearly unchanged (15.97→16.16 µs). The L2 hit rate did not improve (36.5%→34.58%), confirming the gain came from reduced predicated branch overhead and better tail-wave distribution rather than cache locality. The swizzle increased registers per thread (30→40), reducing theoretical occupancy from 100% to 75% and achieved occupancy from 46.8% to 38.8%, but the instruction-count reduction more than compensated at this occupancy level.
slow_pseudocode:
# Default linear PID ordering
xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
xmask = xindex < xnumel
fast_pseudocode:
# GROUP_SIZE swizzle reorders block execution
pid = tl.program_id(0)
num_blocks = tl.cdiv(xnumel, XBLOCK)
GROUP_SIZE = 16  # Python int; covers ~2 waves on 132-SM H200
num_groups  = tl.cdiv(num_blocks, GROUP_SIZE)
group_id    = pid // GROUP_SIZE
group_off   = pid %  GROUP_SIZE
swizzled_pid = group_off * num_groups + group_id
swizzled_pid = tl.minimum(swizzled_pid, num_blocks - 1)  # clamp partial last group
xoffset = swizzled_pid * XBLOCK
xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
xmask = xindex < xnumel
applicable_when: WorkloadImbalance NCU rule triggered (>5% max/avg active cycle ratio); waves_per_sm is non-integer (partial last wave); warp cycles per issued instruction >9; kernel is pointwise/elementwise with many predicated branches (tl.where chains or masked loads); branch instruction count is high relative to total instructions.
do_not_apply_when: Registers per thread are already >40 before applying the swizzle — the additional register pressure (+8–10 registers observed) will further reduce theoretical occupancy below 75% and may cause spilling. Avoid if achieved occupancy is already <35% and the kernel is latency-bound. Also avoid if waves_per_sm is already an integer (no tail imbalance to fix). Note: the per-kernel NCU duration may not improve even when end-to-end speedup is significant.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: GROUP_SIZE is a Python integer inside the kernel body (not tl.constexpr), which works but prevents autotuning over GROUP_SIZE. The tl.minimum() clamp on swizzled_pid is mandatory to prevent out-of-bounds access in the last partial group. The autotune config set should also be updated to include a lambda grid: `grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)`. The swizzle adds ~8 registers/thread due to the additional integer arithmetic (pid, num_blocks, num_groups, group_id, group_off, swizzled_pid).

strategy_title: Replace float division by constant with reciprocal multiply
strategy_description: When NCU's FPInstructions rule flags a high ratio of non-fused FP32 instructions (e.g., 87.5% non-fused), a common culprit is division by a constant float value (e.g., `x / 4.0`) which emits a high-latency FDIV instruction. Replacing this with multiplication by the exact reciprocal (e.g., `x * 0.25`) eliminates the FDIV and enables the compiler to fuse the multiply into an FMA with subsequent operations. This is mathematically exact for divisors that are powers of 2 (0.25, 0.5, 0.125, etc.) since they are exactly representable in IEEE 754 float32. Note that in this case the per-kernel NCU duration metrics were nearly unchanged (16.0→16.1 µs) while the end-to-end speedup was 1.759x, suggesting the benefit is distributed across the full workload or the NCU snapshot captured a non-representative kernel invocation.
slow_pseudocode:
# avg_pool2d divide-by-constant: emits FDIV (non-fused, high latency)
tmp12 = tl.full([1], 4.0, tl.float32)
tmp13 = (tmp11 / tmp12)  # FDIV instruction
fast_pseudocode:
# Replace with reciprocal multiply: enables FMA fusion
tmp13 = tmp11 * 0.25  # FMUL, fused-eligible with subsequent ops
applicable_when: NCU FPInstructions rule is triggered with a high fraction of non-fused FP32 instructions (>80% non-fused); kernel contains division by a constant float value (e.g., avg_pool normalization by pool area); the divisor is a power of 2 (0.25, 0.5, 0.125, etc.) ensuring exact IEEE 754 representation; kernel is compute-bound or has high ALU pipeline utilization.
do_not_apply_when: The divisor is not exactly representable as a power-of-2 float (e.g., dividing by 3.0 or 6.0 introduces rounding error); the division result is used in a context requiring exact IEEE 754 division semantics (rare in neural network inference); the kernel is purely memory-bound and instruction reduction will not affect latency.
framework_notes: In Triton, `tl.full([1], 4.0, tl.float32)` followed by division creates a non-fused FDIV. Replacing with `x * 0.25` (Python float literal) allows the Triton compiler to emit FMUL and potentially fuse with adjacent FP32 operations into FMA. This pattern commonly appears in avg_pool2d kernels where the pool area (e.g., 2×2=4) is used as a normalizer. The same optimization applies in CUDA C++ by replacing `x / 4.0f` with `x * 0.25f`.

strategy_title: maxnreg=32 cap with PID swizzle yields 1.67x speedup
strategy_description: Adding maxnreg=32 to all autotune configs alongside a GROUP_SIZE=16 PID swizzle produced a 1.67x end-to-end speedup. The PID swizzle halved branch instructions (86K→43K) and dramatically improved cache utilization: L1/TEX hit rate rose from 54.5% to 66.4%, L2 hit rate from 36.7% to 59.7%, and memory throughput from 722 GB/s to 1.48 TB/s. However, the maxnreg=32 cap caused register spilling (MemoryCacheAccessPattern rule triggered, local load/store utilization at 1/32 bytes per sector), increasing Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction from 10.07 to 12.07 and introducing L1TEX scoreboard stalls (42% of stall cycles). The net effect is positive because the cache locality gains from the swizzle dominate, but the spill-induced L1TEX stalls partially offset the occupancy recovery benefit of maxnreg.
fast_pseudocode:

    configs=[
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128},  num_warps=2,  num_stages=1, maxnreg=32),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 256},  num_warps=4,  num_stages=1, maxnreg=32),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 512},  num_warps=8,  num_stages=1, maxnreg=32),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 2048}, num_warps=16, num_stages=1, maxnreg=32),
        # ... all configs have maxnreg=32
    ],
    key=['xnumel'],
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(...):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    num_blocks = tl.cdiv(xnumel, XBLOCK)
    GROUP_SIZE = 16
    num_groups  = tl.cdiv(num_blocks, GROUP_SIZE)
    group_id    = pid // GROUP_SIZE
    group_off   = pid %  GROUP_SIZE
    swizzled_pid = group_off * num_groups + group_id
    swizzled_pid = tl.minimum(swizzled_pid, num_blocks - 1)
    xoffset = swizzled_pid * XBLOCK
    ...
    tl.store(out_ptr + x4, result, mask=xmask)  # eviction_policy removed
applicable_when: AchievedOccupancy rule triggered with large gap between theoretical and achieved occupancy; registers per thread are elevated (>30) due to swizzle or other arithmetic overhead; Block Limit Registers is the binding occupancy constraint; kernel is not already L1TEX-latency-bound before applying maxnreg; PID swizzle is also being applied to improve cache locality simultaneously.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel already has high register pressure causing spilling (MemoryCacheAccessPattern rule triggered before applying maxnreg) — adding maxnreg will worsen spill traffic and increase L1TEX stalls. Avoid if the kernel is already L1TEX scoreboard-stall-dominated (CPIStall L1TEX fraction >40%) since spilling will amplify this bottleneck. Also avoid if the register count is already at or below the target cap (no benefit). Note: the per-kernel NCU duration may increase even when end-to-end speedup is positive, because the swizzle's cache locality benefit is distributed across the workload.
framework_notes: In Triton, maxnreg is a per-Config parameter in triton.Config({'XBLOCK': N}, num_warps=W, num_stages=S, maxnreg=R). It maps to the PTX .maxnreg directive and is enforced by the compiler, causing register spilling to local memory for temporaries exceeding the cap. On Hopper (H200), 65536 registers/SM: at 32 regs/thread × 64 threads/block = 2048 regs/block → 32 blocks/SM → 100% theoretical occupancy. At 40 regs/thread × 64 threads/block = 2560 regs/block → 25 blocks/SM → ~78% theoretical occupancy. The spill traffic appears as uncoalesced local loads/stores in MemoryCacheAccessPattern (1/32 bytes utilized per sector). num_stages=1 is appropriate for pointwise kernels with no software pipelining benefit.
